title: Linking projects to organisational objectives
blurb: Explain why every project must trace back to the organisation's strategy, and how that link is built and kept alive.
question: An outdoor clothing retailer is half way through building a mobile app when its board changes strategy to focus on selling through partner marketplaces. The app is on time and on budget. Why does the project's link to organisational objectives matter here, and what should happen next?

teach.h: Every project should trace back to strategy
teach.body: Organisations set strategic objectives: what they are trying to achieve, such as growing online sales, cutting carbon or improving patient safety. Projects exist to deliver that strategy. Linking a project to organisational objectives means being able to show which objective it serves and how its outputs will contribute. In plain English: if nobody can say which goal a project helps, it is fair to ask why it is being done at all.

teach.caption: Pull on any piece of project work and you should be able to follow the thread all the way up to the vision.

teach.body: Alignment makes sure the right projects are selected and funded in the first place. It means each project's benefits genuinely support strategic objectives, so the investment pays off. It justifies priorities and resources when projects compete for the same people and money. And it lets the organisation spot and stop projects that no longer fit, before more is spent. Aligned projects also keep senior support, because leaders can see why they matter.

teach.caption: A benefits map traces outputs to outcomes to benefits to strategic objectives. Plan it from right to left (start with the objective); deliver it from left to right.

teach.body: Strategy is not fixed. Markets, regulation and leadership change, so a project that fitted perfectly at approval can drift out of line. Kestrel Outdoor's board switches to selling through partner marketplaces. The project manager should raise the impact straight away; the sponsor and board then review the business case at a decision gate and choose to re-scope, pause or close. Closing a project that no longer fits is good governance, not failure: it frees money for work that does.

teach.h: Keeping the link: linear and iterative

rows.label: Fit checked
values: In the business case, then at each decision gate
Every iteration, as the backlog is reprioritised

rows.label: Who steers
values: Product owner, within the sponsor's goals

teach.text: Exam trap: 'the project was on time, on budget and to specification, so it succeeded'. Not if its outputs no longer contribute to strategic objectives. Also watch for options that treat alignment as a one-off check at approval: it must be re-checked throughout the life cycle.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State the principle: projects exist to deliver organisational strategy and objectives.
Explain why it is important: right projects funded, benefits support objectives, priorities justified, misfits stopped.
Describe how the link is made: business case, sponsor, benefits map, portfolio prioritisation.
Explain how it is maintained: reviews at decision gates (linear) or each iteration (iterative).
Apply it to the scenario: what the change in strategy means and who should decide what happens.
Projects exist to deliver strategy; each should show which objective it serves.
Alignment means the right projects are funded, benefits support objectives and resources are justified.
Benefits map: outputs, then outcomes, then benefits, then strategic objectives.
Alignment is kept alive through the business case, sponsor, portfolio and decision gates.
When strategy changes, re-check the project; stopping a misfit early is good governance.

summary: You can now explain why linking projects to organisational objectives matters: the right work is funded, benefits support the strategy, and projects that no longer fit are stopped. You can also describe how the link is built and maintained through the business case, benefits mapping, the sponsor, the portfolio and regular reviews.

A.q: What is the MAIN reason for linking projects to an organisation's objectives?
options: To make the project plan easier to write
To give the project team more autonomy
To avoid the need for a business case
To ensure investment delivers the strategy
A.why: Projects exist to deliver strategy. Linking them to objectives makes sure money and effort go into work that moves the organisation where it wants to go.

whyNot.0: Alignment is about value and direction, not making planning documents easier.
whyNot.1: Alignment can actually constrain a team's choices to what serves the strategy.
whyNot.2: The business case is one of the main ways the strategic link is shown, so it is still needed.

A.q: Which document MOST directly shows a project's strategic fit when it is approved?
A.why: The business case justifies the project, including how it contributes to the organisation's strategic objectives.

whyNot.0: The risk register records uncertain events, not the strategic justification.
whyNot.2: The issue log records problems that have already happened.
whyNot.3: The lessons log records learning for future work.

A.q: Which sequence correctly shows how a project's work contributes to strategy?
A.why: Outputs are used to create outcomes; outcomes give measurable benefits; benefits contribute to strategic objectives.

whyNot.1: Benefits come from outcomes, which come from outputs, so benefits cannot come first.
whyNot.2: Objectives are the end point the chain contributes to, not the start of delivery.
whyNot.3: Outcomes arise from using outputs, so outputs must come first.

B.q: Half way through building a new regional depot, a logistics firm's board announces it will deliver everything from one central hub, making regional depots unnecessary. What should happen FIRST?
options: Finish the depot, since it is half built
Ask the team to work faster to finish it
Review the business case at a decision gate
Keep going and report the change at closure
B.why: A change in strategy may remove the project's justification, so the business case should be reviewed and the sponsor and board decide whether to re-scope, pause or close.

whyNot.0: Money already spent is not a reason to keep spending on work that no longer fits the strategy.
whyNot.1: Finishing faster just completes an output nobody needs.
whyNot.3: Waiting until closure wastes the chance to stop or redirect spending now.

B.q: A project is on time, on budget and meeting its quality targets, but its outputs no longer support any strategic objective. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: It is unlikely to be judged a success overall
It is a success, as time, cost and quality are met
It should continue so the spend is not wasted
It is now the project manager's to re-scope
B.why: Meeting time, cost and quality is not enough: a project that no longer contributes to strategic objectives delivers little value.

whyNot.1: Time, cost and quality measure delivery, not whether the work is worth doing.
whyNot.2: Continuing to spend on work with no strategic value wastes more money.
whyNot.3: Re-scoping is a sponsor and board decision; the project manager raises the issue.

B.q:
Which TWO are benefits of aligning projects with organisational objectives?
1) The right projects are selected and funded
2) Projects no longer need decision gates
3) Resources go to the highest priorities
4) The sponsor role becomes unnecessary
B.why: Alignment helps select and fund the right projects and justifies giving resources to the highest strategic priorities.

whyNot.0: Decision gates are still needed; they are one of the ways alignment is re-checked.
whyNot.1: Gates and the sponsor are both part of how alignment is kept alive.
whyNot.2: Resources going to priorities is right, but the sponsor remains essential.

C.q: In an iterative project, who MOST directly keeps the work aligned with business value from one iteration to the next?
C.why: The product owner represents the business and prioritises the backlog by value each iteration, within the sponsor's objectives.

whyNot.0: Auditors provide independent assurance; they do not prioritise the backlog.
whyNot.2: Developers build the work but do not own the business priorities.
whyNot.3: Finance tracks money, not the value order of the backlog.

C.q: A retailer has 25 change projects running. Its new strategy focuses entirely on online growth. Which action BEST demonstrates linking projects to objectives?
options: Let every project finish as first planned
Cut every budget by the same percentage
Re-prioritise projects by fit to strategy
Favour the projects that started earliest
C.why: Re-prioritising by strategic fit directs resources to projects that support online growth and exposes those that should be stopped.

whyNot.0: Ignoring the new strategy keeps funding work that may no longer fit.
whyNot.1: Equal cuts ignore which projects actually contribute to the strategy.
whyNot.3: Start date says nothing about strategic value.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism for keeping projects aligned with strategy?
options: Decision gate reviews by a board
C.why: A resource histogram shows resource demand over time. It is a planning tool and says nothing about strategic fit.

whyNot.1: Benefits mapping traces outputs through to strategic objectives.
whyNot.2: Decision gates re-check the business case, including strategic fit.
whyNot.3: Portfolio prioritisation ranks work by its contribution to strategy.

reteach.title: A football club chasing promotion
reteach.question: A football club's goal this season is promotion. The owners have money for a few big decisions: a new striker, a new stadium bar, a youth academy. How does 'linking projects to objectives' work for the club?

blocks.h: Does it help us win promotion?
blocks.body: Every spending decision is tested against the season's objective. Signing a striker clearly helps: more goals, more points. A smart new bar may be pleasant but does nothing for promotion this year, so it waits. If the club changes its goal mid-season (survival instead of promotion), the manager re-checks every plan. A striker who never plays is like a project nobody uses: money spent, objective missed.

blocks.text: A signing completed on time and under budget is still a poor decision if it does not help the club's objective. Delivery alone is not success.

explain.body: Vision and mission set strategic objectives. The portfolio invests in change to meet them. Programmes and projects deliver that change. You should be able to trace any project's work back up to an objective.

test.q: What does the 'golden thread' in project alignment describe?
options: The project's critical path through tasks
The chain of command in a matrix team
The order in which risks are escalated
The link from strategy down to project work
test.why: The golden thread is the traceable link from the organisation's vision and objectives down to the work a project does.

whyNot.0: The critical path is a scheduling idea: the longest chain of dependent activities.
whyNot.1: Reporting lines in a matrix are about organisation structure, not strategic fit.
whyNot.2: Escalation routes are part of risk and issue management.

explain.body: Alignment gets the right projects funded, makes benefits support strategic objectives, justifies priorities and resources, and lets misfits be stopped early. Without it, scarce money and people drift into low-value work.

test.q: Which is a likely consequence of POOR alignment between projects and strategy?
options: Faster approval for every new proposal
Scarce resources spent on low-value work
Stronger senior support for all projects
test.why: Without alignment, money and people are spread across work that does little for the strategy.

whyNot.0: Poor alignment makes approvals harder to justify, not faster.
whyNot.2: Senior support usually fades for projects that do not clearly serve the strategy.
whyNot.3: Misaligned work adds to competition for resources rather than reducing it.

explain.body: A benefits map shows the chain: outputs (what is built) lead to outcomes (what changes when they are used), which give benefits (measurable improvements), which contribute to strategic objectives.

test.q: Kestrel Outdoor's new app is live, and customers now reorder through it. In a benefits map, 'customers reorder through the app' is best described as what?
test.why: An outcome is the changed behaviour or circumstance that results from using an output.

whyNot.0: The output is the app itself.
whyNot.1: The benefit is the measurable improvement that follows, such as higher repeat sales.
whyNot.3: The objective is the strategic goal, such as growing online revenue.

explain.body: Strategy can shift during a project. The project manager raises the impact; the sponsor and board review the business case, often at a decision gate, and decide to continue, re-scope, pause or close.

test.q: Who would normally decide whether a project that no longer fits the strategy should be closed?
test.why: The sponsor owns the business case and, with the board, takes decisions about continuing or closing the project.

whyNot.0: The project manager raises the issue but this decision is beyond their authority.
whyNot.1: The team delivers the work; it does not decide the project's future.
whyNot.2: A supplier has no authority over the client's strategic decisions.
